mathematics_checks: Checked the pinned primary source, Chewi Lectures on Optimization arXiv:2605.07006v1, Exercise 3.3 (https://arxiv.org/html/2605.07006v1#S3, lines 676–678) and Theorem 3.4, (3.2) and its h = 1/β specialization (lines 557–566, 604–610). The exercise ranges over positive-definite quadratics and sharpness tests for the section; this is one scalar function-value order component. For N ≥ 1 the convex specialization at initial distance one gives β/(2N). The explicit witness, bound constant and pointwise comparison are the item's original analysis, not attributed as quoted source results.

For D = N+1 ≥ 1, 0 < μ = β/(2D) ≤ β, f′(x) = μx and f″ = μ. The exact Taylor remainder is (μ/2)(y−x)², so f minus the strong-convexity quadratic is identically zero and β bounds the upper model. The derivative is also β-Lipschitz by μ ≤ β, as needed to specialize the source upper bound. Positivity gives the unique minimizer 0.

T(x) = qx for q = 1−1/(2D) ∈ [1/2,1); T^[N](1) = q^N, including N = 0. Bernoulli on q^N gives 1−N/(2D) = (D+1)/(2D) ≥ 1/2. Both sides are nonnegative, so squaring and multiplying by β/(4D) gives β/(16D); the exact gap is β/(4D) q^(2N). At N = 0 it is β/4; no N = 0 claim is made for the source upper bound.

For fixed β, the supremum over 0 < μ ≤ β at each N is at least β/(16D), hence its ratio to β/D is at least 1/16 at every horizon. Any putative class-uniform bound with ratio tending to zero is impossible; for N ≥ 1 the lower estimate is also ≥ β/(32N). There is no conflict with fixing μ first: r = 1−μ/β lies in [0,1), the gap is μr^(2n)/2, and at r = 0 it vanishes after one step. For r > 0, consecutive terms of (n+1)r^(2n) have ratio ((n+2)/(n+1))r² → r² < 1, giving eventual geometric domination and the stated little-o.
